rows.verified: Respiratory protective equipment must be adequate for the hazard and suitable for the wearer, task and environment.
RPE selection should account for the wearer, the work task and the environment in which it will be used.
RPE should normally be a last line of protection after exposure has been controlled by other reasonably practicable measures such as LEV.
RPE may be needed for spill response, maintenance, temporary control failure, cleaning, short one-off work or as additional protection.
Each wearer must be fit tested for each tight-fitting RPE facepiece they use.
RPE must work compatibly with other protective equipment worn by the user.
Wearers must be trained and supervised, and RPE must be maintained according to manufacturer instructions and stored correctly.
The two main RPE types are respirators that filter contaminated air and breathing apparatus supplied with breathing-quality air from an independent source.
RPE suitability depends on the contaminant, airborne form, concentration, oxygen level, wearer, task, duration and other PPE.
RPE evidence is hazard-, wearer- and task-specific and is not an exact parcel-level respiratory-disease probability.
Work-related skin disease can be caused or worsened by chemicals, products and prolonged wet work.
Dermatitis is the most common work-related skin problem, while urticaria and skin cancer can also occur.
The APC approach begins by avoiding direct contact through elimination, substitution or tools and equipment that create a safe working distance.
Where contact cannot be avoided, employers should provide suitable skin protection such as correctly selected gloves.
Glove selection should consider the substances, other hand hazards, contact type and duration, user size and comfort, and the task.
No glove material protects against every substance and no glove protects indefinitely against a particular substance.
Skin-protection arrangements should include suitable washing facilities, mild cleaners, thorough drying and regular moisturising.
Regular skin checks help identify early dermatitis, support prompt treatment and show whether exposure controls remain adequate.
Skin controls depend on the substance, contact route, wet-work duration, task, glove compatibility, worker sensitivity and hygiene practices.
Skin-exposure evidence is substance-, task- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level dermatitis or cancer probability.
